criteria_quotes: Aetna considers total ankle arthroplasty (TAA) using a Food and Drug Administration-cleared implant ... medically necessary when the following criteria are met: TAA is used to replace an arthritic or severely degenerated ankle; and Member is skeletally mature; and Member has ... moderate or severe pain with loss of ankle mobility and function; and Imaging is consistent with severe arthritis / degeneration of the ankle due to osteoarthritis (degenerative arthritis), post-traumatic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or inflammatory arthritis; and Member has ... failed at least 6 months of conservative management (including physical therapy by a licensed physical therapist, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and orthoses as indicated); and If member is diabetic, their hemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) should be less than 8 percent within 3 months prior to surgery; and Member has none of the contraindications to TAA listed below: [list of ~20 contraindications, e.g. active/prior deep infection, avascular necrosis of the talus, Charcot joint, intra-articular corticosteroid injection within 12 weeks of planned arthroplasty, severe osteoporosis/osteopenia, vascular insufficiency, prior ankle arthrodesis, severe hindfoot/forefoot or knee malalignment, skeletal immaturity, etc.]

Footnote1: Physical therapy (in-person as opposed to home or virtual physical therapy) must be recent (within the past year), for at least 6 weeks (12 weeks with age less than 50 years or BMI greater than 40), and needs to be confirmed either by the actual PT notes, or by documentation in the member claims history. Conservative therapy may be inappropriate and not required for severe osteoarthritis with bone-on-bone articulation in the weight-bearing portion of the joint.

Aetna considers revision TAA medically necessary for individuals with failed total ankle prosthesis. Aetna considers TAA experimental, investigational, or unproven for all other indications because its effectiveness for indications other than the ones listed above has not been established.

{"url": "https://www.aetna.com/cpb/medical/data/600_699/0645.html#", "final_url": "https://www.aetna.com/cpb/medical/data/600_699/0645.html", "http_status": 200, "content_type": "text/html", "login_wall": false, "blocked": false, "blocked_reason": null, "error": null, "text": "Total Ankle Arthroplasty - Medical Clinical Policy Bulletins | Aetna --> Top Total Ankle Arthroplasty Clinical Policy Bulletins Medical Clinical Policy Bulletins Print Share Number: 0645 Table Of Contents Policy Applicable CPT / HCPCS / ICD-10 Codes Background References Policy Scope of Policy This Clinical Policy Bulletin addresses total ankle arthroplasty. Note: Precertification may be required for select procedures and interventions. Use the CPT code search tool to see if precertification is required. Medical Necessity Aetna considers total ankle arthroplasty (TAA) using a Food and Drug Administration-cleared implant (e.g., the Agility LP Total Ankle, the Eclipse Total Ankle, the INBONE Total Ankle, the Infinity Total Ankle System, the STAR system, the Salto Talaris Total Ankle Prosthesis, and the Zimmer Trabecular Metal Total Ankle) medically necessary when the following criteria are met: TAA is used to replace an arthritic or severely degenerated ankle; and Member is skeletally mature; and Member has with moderate or severe pain with loss of ankle mobility and function; and Imaging is consistent with severe arthritis / degeneration of the ankle due to osteoarthritis (degenerative arthritis), post-traumatic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or inflammatory arthritis; and Member has have failed at least 6 months of conservative management (including physical therapy Footnote1 * by a licensed physical therapist, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and orthoses as indicated); and If member is diabetic, their hemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) should be less than 8 percent within 3 months prior to surgery; and Member has none of the contraindications to TAA listed below: Absence of the medial or lateral malleolus Active or prior deep infection in the ankle joint or adjacent bones Avascular necrosis of the talus Charcot joint Corticosteroid injection into the joint within 12 weeks of the planned arthroplasty Hindfoot or forefoot mal-alignment precluding plantigrade foot Insufficient bone or musculature such that proper component positioning or alignment is not possible Insufficient ligament support that can not be repaired with soft tissue stabilization Lower extremity vascular insufficiency Neuromuscular disease resulting in lack of normal muscle function about the affected ankle Osteonecrosis Peripheral neuropathy (may lead to Charcot joint of the affected ankle) Poor skin and soft tissue quality about the surgical site Prior arthrodesis (fusion) at the ankle joint Prior surgery or injury that has adversely affected ankle bone quality Psychiatric problems that hinder adequate cooperation during peri-operative period Severe anatomic deformity in adjacent ankle structures, including hindfoot, forefoot and knee joint Severe ankle deformity (e.g., severe varus or valgus deformity) that would not normally be eligible for ankle arthroplasty Severe osteoporosis, osteopenia or other conditions resulting in poor bone quality, as this may result in inadequate bony fixation Significant mal-alignment of the knee joint Skeletal maturity not yet reached Vascular insufficiency in the affected limb. Footnote1 * Physical therapy (in-person as opposed to home or virtual physical therapy) must be recent (within the past year), for at least 6 weeks (12 weeks with age less than 50 years or BMI greater than 40), and needs to be confirmed either by the actual PT notes, or by documentation in the member claims history. Conservative therapy may be inappropriate and not required for severe osteoarthritis with bone-on-bone articulation in the weight-bearing portion of the joint. Aetna considers revision TAA medically necessary for individuals with failed total ankle prosthesis. Aetna considers TAA experimental, investigational, or unproven for all other indications because its effectiveness for indications other than the ones listed above has not been established. Experimental, Investigational, or Unproven Aetna considers the following procedures experimental, investigational, or unproven because the effectiveness of these approaches has not been established: Combined total ankle arthroplasty and total talar prosthesis for end-stage osteoarthritis of the ankle and other indications Custom implants for total ankle arthroplasty Incisional negative pressure wound therapy applied after total ankle arthroplasty Intra-operative fresh frozen section analysis to determine the presence of infection during total ankle arthroplasty Total talar replacement for end-stage avascular necrosis of the talus, and all other indications Trans-fibular total ankle arthroplasty.
